This is one that I use in class as a counterpoint to all of the 1950s Technocolor Fantasy footage found elsewhere in the archives. My students are mostly African-American, and the way my unit on the '50s in my textbook is set up, it goes point/counterpoint, with all of the Happy Days sorts of images and features of American life (prosperous, cool, and above all, very, very white) balanced against the poverty, opression and racisim that went on at the same time. The '50s was a bright, shiny lid clamped on a seething cauldron of social ills. When the lid pops off in the '60s, it isnt pretty...…

I am a 58 year old white woman from Texas. And, after seeing this film, I can say without a doubt, if I had my choice to sit on the porch and talk to a family and pass the time, I would pick anyone in this film over the folks in the white-bread perfection world of most of these 1950's Coronet films. I agree with History Teacher's Assessment of this film completely.

I think the publication date of this film is incorrect. This film was cited in catalogues and educational reports of the early 1950s. The right date is probably 1949/50. It is a peculiar one among educational films of the 50s. There were no black families represented in almost all of them.
Stilted Effort nonetheless rings somewhat true

The point of this film was to instruct parents how to raise their children properly. The storyline that asks how the mother/children will carry on if the father (bread winner) is incapacitated is handled in a truly hoakie way, however, before that final/forced plot twist, I truly enjoyed seeing city Negroes going about their family life and work life in ways that don't fit either minstrel, blaxploitation or hip hop stereotypes. The elemenyd are believable to me: the humble surroundings; the proud father; the self-righteous aunt; the mother who also works; and the dramatizations of how…
"HEY YOU KIDS! GET OFF THE PORCH!"

Curious hybrid of soap opera, history lesson, race relation film, melodrama AND coronet instructional film about a poor family growing up in the South. The Mother stays at home all day (save for a part time job) the father also has a full time job, and they have 4 hungry mouths to feed. All the acting here is pretty amazing. It looks obvious that the kids don't appear to be acting, as it looks like this is an actual family we're seeing. I would've liked to have kept the documentary thing going and not verge into soap opera territory ("Your husband's been hurt REAL bad!") but that's a bit of a…

anglosaxonengland: Archeological adviser, Stanley E. West Outlines English history from the end of Roman rule around 410 to the Norman invasion in 1066. Presents the various raids and migrations which changed the face of England; details the settlements of the Anglo-Saxons by recent excavations at Cadbury, West Stow, and Winchester; and portrays the growth of the monasteries

rv: With the advent of Covid I've been looking at the history of Plagues which swept through England, and the rest of the word and... I'm noticing that only a very few plagues, such as swept London in 1665 (Hence: Ring'a'Ring of Roses) are ever menioned... And yes, there were many, many plagues between Saxon Times and Right Now in what could be called "The Middle Of A Plague".

Wilbur_Gets_The_Message: Wilbur is persuaded of the merits of Payroll Savings bonds, with a cameo by Mister Ed; a 1964 Treasury promotional film.

rv: Good for historical purposes but like so many of the sit-com of the time, Mr. Ed is kind of difficult to watch. This little flick is actually quite irksome.

BrokenGlass: Interprets the hazards inherent to the intersection, using staged collisions with anthropomorphic dummies.

rv: A bit of a classic film here as this film I believe introduces the Crash Test Dummy footage of two cars colliding with each other. They do it from multiple angles, and it is quite riveting. I think I saw this film, or something close to it, in elementary school and we were all hooting and hollering at the poor demises of the CTDs.

The 'present day' scenes in this film are from the early 1960s. The latest model year car in the street scenes is about 1963. So, I would guess it is from about 1964. The beginning of the film is missing.
a variety show in its prime

Classic variety show by Garry Moore. Moore had been a straight man for Jimmy Durante in the 1940's before CBS picked him up for his own shows on radio and television. Here he is joined by announcer and friend Durwood Kirby. Marion Lorne and up and coming talent Carol Burnett round out the supporting cast. Guest stars are Robert Goulet, Julie London and Bob Newhart. The Johnson's Wax ads are out but an ad remains for the Polaroid Electric Eye Land Camera. During the *That Wonderful Year* segment highlighting 1947, there is a quirky moment where Bob Newhart does a verse of Dusty Fletcher's Open…

HMStLouisAreaFami97470: Viewing notes state: Religious site with Stations of the Cross Post office Girls with dolls Grandpa with Ritz at kitchen table card playing 8mm movie projector Homemade quilts and dresses Navy airport (short) Folks with booze Halloween costumes Girl with doll Farm with piglets Living room dancers - grandpa with granddaughter Christmas with dolls Young soldier

rv: Lots and lots of shots with this family. The highlights are those neutral 60's Halloween costumes, not that scary then, but scary as hell now. Plenty of fun had at various parties here too. A girl gets a Bingo game for a present!

ClassicT1948_8: Collection of TV commercials significant to the history and development of TV as an advertising medium.

rv: This has been my favorite of the classic commercials collections. All of the concepts in these ads are still pretty modern (Maxwell House has used that song in recent years), but the retro look and music makes it really fun to watch. Surely the Butternut Coffee commercial was done by Jay Ward? Or it was at least meant to look like Rocky and Bullwinkle

Where is Volume VII? I love watching these commercials. So many memories come just come flooding back (Maybe I watched too much TV as a kid?...). I remember some of these better than the shows they sponsored. Thanks, Warren
The hilarious "subliminal" coffee ad has got to be the work of the legendary Stan Freberg. Cracker Jack guy is of course Jack Gilford ("Cocoon") -- I remember this ad from when I was a kid!

Great ads, but these are late '50s to early-mid '60s. We had a '62 Impala convertible that looked a lot like the car in that Hertz ad. I recall the Cracker Jacks ad, and the rest of that series in the mid-late '60s as well. All of these are great examples of the period. BTW the movie Good Neighbor Sam (1963), partly set in an ad agency, contains several spoofs of those Hertz commercials that "put you in the drivers seat".

ChardonJeans1980TVAd: Chardon Jeans commercial, from the Jeans History Project's collection of denim advertising.
TommyLoughranVsJamesBraddock: Boxing. Championship. Tommy Loughran vs James Braddock. Jul. 18, 1929. Yankee Stadium, Bronx, New York, United States.

rv: A great interpretation of Holmes and Watson

It's great to see a pair of actors playing Holmes and Watson who are NOT trying to channel Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce, but who instead bring their own interpretation of these characters to the boards. Although made with a low budget, a good company of players, loving attention to details from the canon (like the gasogene and tantulus on the side-board, the picture of General Gordon, etc.) and great cinematography more than make up for any deficiencies of budget. A refreshing take on classic characters, I only wish they had made more of them....

Warm and funny, this sherlock may not be traditional, but is comforting to watch and entertaining. Humor is a focus here more than most other interpretations bother with and his relationship with watson is actually believabe as a friendship. The skits are short and easy with plenty of cheese. My favorite episode is with a young "alfred pennyworth" where the tensions are high. Sherlock tries to find where the bodies are hidden and almost runs out of time. A bit macabre, i love how the actors play off each other. "Alfred" has such a calm and confident menace. Its great.

I see we have comments from the shallow end of the gene pool here. This series was made by an American production company, many directed by German-American director Steve Previn, others by Americans Jack Gage, with scripts written by Americans for American television, and was shown to American audiences. Much like many British B horror movies of the 1950s-60s that were made in Eastern Europe with local technical staff and actors for all but the starring roles. And much like many classic Hollywood movies that used British actors in starring roles.

Heartand1937: Classic educational film on the workings of the circulatory system from ERPI Classroom Films Inc..

rv: If you are looking for a campy edu-film this one is not it. PETA would have a collective stroke if someone tried to release this film today. "Mr. Hemoglobin" is deals with the subject matter in a far better (more camp - no dead animals) manner. My recommendation is to wait until someone uploads the latter.

The other is an older man, influential in the affairs of Austria, who could provide wealth...and tender devotion. Hannerl thinks about it.

Martinez1927: Scenes shot in Martinez, Contra Costa County, California, on San Pablo Bay, apparently in the late 1920s. Images include: pans over the waterfront; workers at the Bay Specialty Company; the erection of the American Plywood factory; white-collar men exiting a meeting, greeting the camera and tipping their hats; workers at the Martinez Steam Laundry posing; flappers outside another business; entrance to Alhambra Union High School and students leaving; high-school girls in typing class; Martinez…

rv: Really interesting for the clothing of the era for work clothes, office clothes, sports clothes, and school clothes. Very clear and predates sound with film. In the football scene, we see the shadow of the camera man moving to make the roll turn! It is really hilarious to see the kids move their Charlie Chaplin mustaches and walk around with oversized shoes.
Where were going, we dont need roads..

Somewhat primitive, it sort of reminded me of the Besse rolls, but this of course was filmed in 1927, so everything was just a tad bit dirtier, of the town of Martinez California. My guess is, is that this was a town that was truly blessed to have the railroad run through it, because, while there may be SOME signs of progress. It still appeared to be a mud and muck kind of town. This was a very interesting reel, as we explore social clubs in the city, the schools football teams, some buildings in town, and the schools. Unfortunately the filmmaker spends a wee bit too MUCH time on the school…

tire-au-flanc-jean-renoir-1928-michel-si: Jean Renoir's comedy of military service, with Michel Simon.
1933-10-23_Torpedoes_Launched_From_Air: San Diego: Navy planes from the USS Saratoga, flying a few feet off the water, fire two-thousand-pound torpedoes at moving targets in a demonstration of a new style of sea warfare. Silent.
1918AmericaGoesOver640x480: A film produced and distributed by the US Army Signal Corps during World War I to inform and "educate" the US population about the reasons for fighting the war. Featured are scenes with Gen. John Pershing, commander of US forces in Europe, and views of US soldiers in combat and resting up between battles.
6267MakingTheSynchrophaseInGrebeland0135: An industrial film of the A. H. Grebe company's radio factory: parts machined on the factory floor, and Synchrophase radios assembled by hand by men and women.

rv: The production history of a making of a Synchrophase, or a radio for all you simple folk, is shown here, There's some lovely 1920s assembly line footage here, All the big jobs are handled by men of course, but there are women further down the chain though, assembling little things. i also admire the tiny bit dangerous machines they got going there with their bare hands. Eek!

0927_Canning_Cold_Pack_Method_14_52_29_1: A demonstration of the One Period Cold Pack Method of home canning, as approved by the U.S. Government, for viewers unfamiliar with how simple it is.

rv: Good as a look into a period kitchen. Should anyone be using this as a how-to...don't can meat or fish like this film shows. You need a pressure cooker to get temperatures high enough to kill dangerous micro-organisms in meat canning.

InOurHan1950: How economic progress comes from the accumulation of privately owned tools of production; demonstrates the need for tools by showing a young couple with their infant child in a wilderness with nothing but natural resources and their hands.

rv: Excellent critique of the collectivist argument

Actually a fairly accurate description of American exceptionalism, and the tricky methodologies used by Marxist regimes both to gain power and to consolidate their authority once in power. The third film is especially well though out, as it apparently uses the historical experience of Ukranian kulaks and the like to describe how a Marxist regime operates in practice - I'm sure plenty of Venezuelan employees of Prevenza, or disenfranchised industrial farmers from Rhodesia, would find plenty to recognise from the narrative. The commentary about a plebiscite to throw out the national…

I'd definatly suggest reading up on your history before watching this. Perhaps read Howard Zinn's: A People's History of the U.S., or if you are lazy and don't read like most Americans (they way they like us), then I would highly suggest watching the PBS mini-series: Race - The power of an Illusion... at least the second video, it will give you a crash course on accurate American history and objectives. Finally come back to this video and you will see a nightmare rather than just mere history. A far cry from the teachings of Jesus if anything.
We Got what We Have From Being Americans! (snicker)

A truly bizarre mindfuck of a short. This odd little ditty crams so much information into it's 20 minute time frame that your head starts to hurt. At first it's a finger point at all the bad men in their communist countries, like Hitler, Mao, Mussolini, you know those guys. From there, the film seems to take a 180 degree turn and goes 'Survivor' on us by taking a husband and wife and baby and taking away everything they take for granted, housing, food, clothing and we get to watch them duke it out for themselves. Very bizarre. The film goes back to 'normal' and we see What Makes America So…
How we lie about what we got

A twisted 20 minute attempt to explain that the Industrial Revolution was due to the rights outlined in the Declaration of Independence. The proof: post World War 2 statistics about the industrial power of the United States (never mind that the US, the UK, the USSR, Germany, and Japan bombed the hell out of the rest of the industrialized world). Dramatized section a third of the way through throws a modern family into a world without civilization and bears no logical connection to the rest, and for that alone it's worth a view.
Yikes! The Very Thought of Getting My Hands Dirty!

Not me. I'm gonna spend 40K on college and work in a cubicle collating checklists for lawyers and the IRS to use. One day I'll be a GS-7 by God! Let China worry about making things and stuff. We'll just outlaw all that dirty nonsense here. Who needs it? We just print money. Way easier. Shows a Euro white couple after Islam completes its conquest of the developed world. I guess they are in hiding because she lost her burka. Scary, isn't it? This short will bewilder many, I presume.

Weird little film---one of a series produced by Borg Warner and Inland Steel at the dawn of the McCarthy era---purporting to tell us why we Americans are so great! Why, we have 50% of the world's productive capacity! I'm sure the fact that, in 1950, the rest of the industrialized world was just starting to rebuild after the war had nothing to do with it! There's a strange interlude showing how tough life would be without farms, factories and housing (duh!) which is disconnected from the apparent point of the film. The star, by the way, is the guy who later played Sky King---"Out of the clear…

BflOggGX1963: Spoofy look at the motion-picture production process, made to encourage discussion among filmmakers.

rv: After being around this profession for few years, I found this video quite motivational. Funny reactions of chimps reminds me of how we do feel in crazy situations. Haven't anyone felt like the chimp on the moviola after watching impossible-to-edit takes? Haven't any sound engineer felt the same after several hours of shooting and reshooting same scene? In few words: if you feel down, watch this!
As written below: "a silly and humorous look at the film-making industry with a cast of monkeys. Not really meant to be taken seriously" Yes, indeedy!

This film could have easily gotten a 4 or even a five from me, the premise was thier (a bunch of monkeys working in the film industry) but it's brought down by one main factor: thier are large gaps of time between the different scenes.This is unacceptable, and I'm surprised know one at the studio where this was produced did anything about it. Still you can't go wrong with monkys it's an intresting premise but not very well executed.
This is a silly and humorous look at the film-making industry with a cast of monkeys. Not really meant to be taken seriously, this is a interesting look into 70's filmmaking.
Not terribly amusing look at film making that gets a boost from an adorable cast of chimps and some great old office furniture.

rv: I always enjoy the Gould cans.. Little slices of history, though not really very important. Here we see a pack of girls off to summer camp. What kind of camp? Who knows, they seem well off though. I don't trust that wagon they're on though.

The dance sequences are memorable as are the girl's costumes. Like most of the Soundies here, this film needs to be reversed. With the above caveats - Recommended.

This is a very interesting piece. The song is pretty standard (actually, it's a fairly fun song) and the soundie is fun as usual, with lots of dancing girls in short skirts, some rather curious male dancers (why ARE they holding out their hand? for her snot rag?) and a pretty good, but unspectacular singer. rv: Oh! To be in Paris in 1937!

Nice gorgeous tour of the Paris exposition here. We see the Eiffel being the center of attention, and yes, I did actually look up to make sure I was right about it being built... before this exposition (I was right!). We explore the exteriors of many buildings. They're not bad, but nowhere near the glory of Chicago or New York's world fairs. Norway's is the best in my view. After that, we take an extended boat ride, and then more exhibits. Finally, we hit the midway, and oh my! The rides!
